title: Does Alcohol Raise Cholesterol? HDL, LDL and Triglycerides
excerpt: Does alcohol raise cholesterol? How drinking affects HDL, LDL, and triglycerides, how long to skip alcohol before a lipid test, statins, and what cutting back changes.
metaDescription: Does alcohol raise cholesterol? How drinking affects HDL, LDL and triglycerides, when to skip it before a lipid test, and what cutting back changes.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol doesn't raise "cholesterol" as one number. It pushes the different parts of your cholesterol panel in different directions. Drinking tends to **raise HDL** (the "good" cholesterol) a little, has **only a small and inconsistent effect on LDL** (the "bad" cholesterol) at moderate amounts, and **raises triglycerides**, sometimes a lot. Heavy drinking is where the damage concentrates: high triglycerides, a stressed liver, weight gain, and higher blood pressure. And the small HDL bump that drinking gives you probably doesn't protect your heart the way people once hoped.

**The quick rules:** Don't start drinking to improve your cholesterol, because no major heart organization recommends it. If your triglycerides are high, alcohol is one of the first things worth cutting back, and the effect often shows up within weeks. Skip alcohol for at least a day or two before a cholesterol blood test, or your triglyceride result may come back higher than your usual level. If you take a statin, light drinking is usually fine, but heavy drinking is not, so ask your doctor what's reasonable for you.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and blood fats. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your history and your lab results. **See a doctor if** your triglycerides have come back above 500 mg/dL, you have a family history of very high cholesterol or early heart disease, you take a statin or another cholesterol drug and drink more than a little, or you've been told your liver enzymes are high. **Get emergency care right away** if you have severe, constant pain in your upper belly that spreads to your back, especially with vomiting, after drinking. That can be pancreatitis, and very high triglycerides plus alcohol are a known trigger.

## Cholesterol in Plain Words: What the Numbers on Your Panel Mean

Cholesterol is a waxy fat your body needs to build cells and make hormones. Your liver makes most of it. Because fat doesn't mix with blood, it travels around your body packed inside protein "carriers" called lipoproteins. The standard blood test, called a lipid panel, measures a few of these:

- **LDL (low-density lipoprotein).** Often called "bad" cholesterol. LDL particles can work their way into artery walls and help build the plaque that narrows arteries. Lower is better.
- **HDL (high-density lipoprotein).** Often called "good" cholesterol, because it helps carry cholesterol away from the arteries and back to the liver. Higher numbers have long been linked with lower heart risk.
- **Triglycerides.** A different kind of fat, the form your body stores extra energy in. They rise after meals and go up with excess calories, sugar, and alcohol.
- **Total cholesterol.** Roughly the sum of LDL, HDL, and a share of triglycerides.

The general adult reference ranges used in the US look like this:

| Measure | Desirable | Borderline | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total cholesterol | Under 200 mg/dL | 200 to 239 | 240 and up |
| LDL | Under 100 (optimal) | 130 to 159 | 160 and up |
| HDL | 60 and up (protective) | 40 to 59 | Under 40 for men, under 50 for women is considered low |
| Triglycerides | Under 150 | 150 to 199 | 200 to 499 high, 500 and up very high |

Your doctor may set different targets depending on your age, diabetes, blood pressure, smoking, and family history. The point here is that "does alcohol raise cholesterol?" has three separate answers, one for each line of the panel that alcohol actually moves.

## How Your Liver Handles Alcohol (and Why Your Blood Fats Change)

Almost all the alcohol you drink is broken down in your liver, and your liver is also your body's main fat factory. That overlap is the whole story.

When your liver processes alcohol, it first turns it into a toxic compound called acetaldehyde, then into acetate. Those reactions use up a helper molecule called NAD+ and leave behind a lot of its partner, NADH. That shift changes how the liver handles fat in two ways:

1. **It burns less fat.** With the chemistry tilted toward NADH, the liver slows down the normal process of burning fatty acids for fuel.
2. **It builds and ships out more fat.** The liver packages more fat as triglycerides and sends it into the blood inside particles called VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein).

Alcohol also carries a lot of calories (about 7 per gram, nearly as many as pure fat), and your body treats alcohol as a fuel to clear first. While it's dealing with the alcohol, the fat and sugar from your meal and your mixers get stored rather than burned.

Over time, regular heavy drinking can leave fat building up inside the liver itself. That's alcohol-related fatty liver, usually the first and most reversible stage of alcohol-related liver disease. If you want the full picture there, see our [fatty liver disease guide](/never-hungover/fatty-liver-disease-complete-guide-causes-symptoms-natural-treatment-2025).

## Does Alcohol Raise Triglycerides? Yes, and This Is the Big One

Of everything on your lipid panel, triglycerides respond to alcohol most clearly.

- **After a single night of drinking,** triglycerides rise in the hours that follow, especially when you drink with a fatty meal. The rise is larger and lasts longer than the one from food alone.
- **With regular drinking,** fasting triglycerides tend to run higher. In people who already have high triglycerides, the effect is often exaggerated, so a moderate amount of alcohol can push them noticeably higher.
- **With heavy drinking,** triglycerides can climb into the very high range. Above about 500 mg/dL, and especially above 1,000, the risk of acute pancreatitis (sudden, painful inflammation of the pancreas) goes up sharply. Alcohol is itself also a leading cause of pancreatitis, so the two together are a bad pairing.

Not everyone responds the same way. Genetics, body weight, diabetes, an underactive thyroid, some medications, and diet all affect how much alcohol moves your triglycerides. Sugary mixers, beer, and cocktails add sugar on top of alcohol, and excess sugar also raises triglycerides.

The encouraging part is that this effect reverses. Clinical guidelines for high triglycerides routinely list limiting or stopping alcohol as one of the first steps, and when people with alcohol-driven high triglycerides stop drinking, their levels usually come down within weeks. For people with very high triglycerides, doctors generally advise avoiding alcohol completely.

## Does Alcohol Raise HDL? Yes, But That's Less Good News Than It Sounds

This is the part that gave alcohol its reputation as "good for your heart."

Drinking does raise HDL, and the effect depends on the dose: more alcohol, a bit more HDL. Controlled feeding studies, where volunteers were given set amounts of alcohol and their blood was tested, found HDL went up by a few mg/dL at around one to two drinks a day. Back when higher HDL was thought to be protective in itself, this looked like a clear benefit.

Two lines of evidence have since cooled that view:

- **Raising HDL with drugs didn't help.** Several drugs that raised HDL by large amounts were tested in big heart trials, and they mostly failed to reduce heart attacks. That suggests the HDL number on its own is more of a marker than a lever. Pushing it up doesn't automatically mean better protection.
- **Genetic studies point the other way.** Researchers have used natural genetic differences that make some people drink less (for example, a common variant of an alcohol-processing gene that makes drinking unpleasant) to study alcohol's effects without the usual biases. People with these variants drink less on average, and in large studies of this kind they've tended to have the same or better heart health, not worse. This kind of study is called Mendelian randomization.

There's also a well-known flaw in the older observational studies that made moderate drinkers look healthier than non-drinkers. The "non-drinker" group often included former drinkers who had quit because they were already sick, and people who drink moderately also tend to be wealthier and more active. When researchers correct for that, much of the apparent benefit shrinks or disappears.

So yes, alcohol raises HDL. But it's not a good reason to drink, and it doesn't cancel out what alcohol does to triglycerides, blood pressure, and weight.

## Does Alcohol Raise LDL Cholesterol?

For most people at light to moderate intake, alcohol has only a small and inconsistent effect on LDL. Some studies find LDL drops slightly with moderate drinking, others find little change. It's not a major driver of LDL the way saturated fat, genetics, and body weight are.

Heavy drinking is a different situation. It can raise LDL and total cholesterol indirectly, through weight gain, a damaged liver that handles fat less well, and the high-fat, late-night food that often comes with a night out. In people with advanced liver disease, cholesterol numbers can do unusual things, which is one more reason to get lab results read by your own doctor.

If your LDL is high, alcohol is usually not the main culprit, and cutting back on drinking alone probably won't fix it. Diet, exercise, weight, genetics, and sometimes medication matter more. But cutting back can still help with the rest of the picture.

## Does Alcohol Raise Total Cholesterol?

Total cholesterol includes HDL, so a drink that bumps up HDL can nudge total cholesterol up slightly even if nothing bad is happening. That's why the total number isn't very useful on its own, and why doctors look at the parts (especially LDL, HDL, and triglycerides) and at "non-HDL cholesterol," which is everything except HDL.

If your total cholesterol is high and you drink regularly, look at the breakdown before deciding what alcohol is doing. A high total driven by HDL is very different from a high total driven by LDL or triglycerides.

## Beer, Wine, or Liquor: Does the Type of Drink Matter?

Less than marketing would suggest. Most of alcohol's effect on blood fats comes from the alcohol itself, so a standard drink of beer, wine, or spirits has broadly similar effects. A "standard drink" in the US is 14 grams of pure alcohol, about 12 oz of regular beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof spirits.

A few differences are real but modest:

- **Beer** adds carbohydrate calories, and large servings add up quickly. Several beers a night is a common route to higher triglycerides and a bigger waistline.
- **Cocktails and mixed drinks** can carry a lot of sugar from juice, soda, and syrups, which adds to the triglyceride effect.
- **Red wine** contains plant compounds like resveratrol and other polyphenols, which get a lot of attention. But the amount in a glass is small, far below the doses used in lab studies, and there is no good evidence that red wine improves cholesterol better than other drinks for the same amount of alcohol.

If you drink, the type matters less than how much and how often. If you want to read more about how different drinks affect you the next day, our [wine drunk vs beer drunk breakdown](/never-hungover/wine-drunk-vs-beer-drunk) covers the overlap.

## Is a Little Alcohol Good for Your Heart? Where the Science Stands Now

For decades, the "J-curve" was the standard story: light drinkers seemed to have fewer heart attacks than non-drinkers, and heavy drinkers had more. The HDL effect was the main proposed reason.

The current view is more cautious:

- The **World Health Organization** stated in 2023 that no level of alcohol use is safe for health, mainly because of alcohol's link to several cancers.
- The **American Heart Association** does not recommend that anyone start drinking to protect their heart. If you don't drink, there's no heart-health reason to begin.
- The **US Dietary Guidelines** advise that adults who choose to drink limit themselves to up to 2 drinks a day for men and up to 1 for women, and that drinking less is better for health than drinking more.

Alcohol also raises blood pressure, a major risk factor for heart attack and stroke, and the effect builds with regular drinking. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) goes into that in detail, and the [alcohol and heart health guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-heart-health-complete-cardiovascular-guide-2025) covers rhythm problems and the rest of the cardiovascular picture.

The practical takeaway: if you enjoy a drink and keep it light, your cholesterol is unlikely to be the thing that suffers most. If your triglycerides, blood pressure, or weight are creeping up, alcohol is one of the easiest things to change.

## Alcohol Before a Cholesterol Test: How Long Should You Wait?

This is one of the most searched questions on the topic, and it matters because a night of drinking can make your results look worse than your real baseline.

- **Triglycerides are the number most affected.** Drinking the evening before a test can push them up, sometimes a lot, especially if you also had a big meal.
- **Many labs and doctors advise avoiding alcohol for at least 24 hours before a lipid test,** and some recommend 48 to 72 hours. Follow whatever instructions your doctor or lab gives you.
- **Fasting rules vary.** Many lipid tests no longer require fasting, but if yours does, it usually means 9 to 12 hours with only water. Alcohol counts as breaking the fast.
- **Be honest with your doctor.** If you drank heavily the night before, tell them. A single high triglyceride reading after a big night out may lead to a repeat test rather than a new prescription.

If your results come back with high triglycerides and you drink regularly, a fair experiment is to cut out alcohol for a few weeks and retest. That tells you and your doctor how much of the number is alcohol and how much is something else.

## Alcohol and Statins

Statins are the most common cholesterol-lowering drugs. They work in the liver, which is also where alcohol is processed, so the combination gets asked about often.

- **Light to moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable** for most people on a statin, but there isn't one rule that fits everyone. Your doctor's advice comes first.
- **Heavy drinking is a concern.** Statin labels caution against use in people who drink substantial amounts of alcohol or have a history of liver disease, because both alcohol and statins can raise liver enzymes in some people.
- **Alcohol works against the reason you're taking the drug.** Heavy drinking raises triglycerides and blood pressure, which undoes some of what the medication is doing.
- **Watch for muscle symptoms.** Unexplained muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine on a statin should be reported to your doctor promptly, whatever your drinking habits.

If you take another lipid-lowering drug, such as a fibrate or niacin, the same general advice applies. Ask your doctor or pharmacist how alcohol fits with your specific medicine.

## Will Cutting Back on Alcohol Lower Your Cholesterol?

It depends on which number you're trying to move.

- **Triglycerides:** often yes, and fairly fast. People whose high triglycerides are driven by drinking can see a meaningful drop within a few weeks of stopping or cutting back.
- **HDL:** it may dip slightly when you drink less. That's expected and isn't a reason to keep drinking.
- **LDL:** usually little direct change, unless cutting back also leads to weight loss and a better diet, which it often does.
- **Liver fat and blood pressure:** both tend to improve with less alcohol, and fatty liver from drinking is often reversible in its early stages.

Weight is a big part of this. Alcohol calories add up quietly, and drinking often comes with extra food. If you're trying to bring your numbers down, our [alcohol and weight loss guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) covers how drinking affects your metabolism.

## Practical Steps If You Drink and Care About Your Cholesterol

1. **Know your numbers.** Get a lipid panel and look at the full breakdown, not just total cholesterol.
2. **Keep drinking light, or skip it.** If you drink, stay within the US guideline limits, and have several alcohol-free days a week.
3. **Watch the sugar in your glass.** Swap sugary mixers for soda water, and go easy on large beer servings.
4. **Don't drink on an empty stomach, but don't pair alcohol with a heavy fried meal either.** Fat and alcohol together drive the biggest triglyceride spikes.
5. **Stop drinking for at least a day or two before a lipid test,** and follow your lab's instructions.
6. **If your triglycerides are high, run a no-alcohol trial.** Several weeks off, then retest, gives you a clear answer.
7. **Talk to your doctor before mixing alcohol with cholesterol medicine** if you drink more than occasionally.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's mainly used to support the body while processing alcohol. It's worth being clear about what it can and can't do for cholesterol.

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers cholesterol or triglycerides in people who drink. One small randomized trial in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease reported improvements in some blood fat and liver markers with DHM, and animal studies on DHM and fat metabolism are promising. But those results haven't been confirmed in larger human trials, and they don't apply to undoing the effects of alcohol on your lipid panel. DHM is not a substitute for drinking less, and it won't replace a statin or any medicine your doctor prescribes.

Where DHM can make sense is as part of a lighter, more careful approach to social drinking. If you'd like to try it, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a straightforward, single-ingredient option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and if you take any cholesterol medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding a supplement. For broader liver support options, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't raise "cholesterol" in one direction. It **raises triglycerides**, **raises HDL slightly**, and has **little consistent effect on LDL** at moderate intake.
- **Triglycerides are the number to watch.** They rise after drinking, rise more with heavy or regular drinking, and come down when you cut back.
- The HDL bump from alcohol **is not a good reason to drink**. Drugs that raise HDL didn't prevent heart attacks, and newer research has weakened the case for drinking for heart health.
- **Skip alcohol for at least 24 hours before a lipid test**, longer if your lab says so.
- **Light drinking is usually compatible with statins; heavy drinking is not.** Ask your doctor about your own situation.
- Severe upper belly pain after drinking, especially with known high triglycerides, needs emergency care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol raise cholesterol?**

Not in a simple way. Alcohol tends to raise triglycerides and HDL ("good") cholesterol, while its effect on LDL ("bad") cholesterol at moderate amounts is small and inconsistent. Heavy drinking can make the overall picture worse through higher triglycerides, weight gain, liver strain, and higher blood pressure.

**Does alcohol raise triglycerides?**

Yes. Triglycerides are the part of your lipid panel most affected by alcohol. They rise in the hours after drinking, run higher in regular drinkers, and can reach very high levels with heavy drinking, which raises the risk of pancreatitis. Cutting back usually brings them down within weeks.

**Does drinking alcohol raise HDL (good) cholesterol?**

Yes, modestly, and more with larger amounts. But raising HDL doesn't appear to protect the heart by itself, because drugs that raised HDL failed to cut heart attacks in large trials. No major heart organization recommends drinking to raise HDL.

**How long should I avoid alcohol before a cholesterol test?**

Many labs and doctors recommend at least 24 hours without alcohol before a lipid test, and some suggest 48 to 72 hours. Alcohol mostly affects your triglyceride result. If your test requires fasting, alcohol breaks the fast. Follow the instructions your doctor or lab gives you.

**Is red wine good for cholesterol?**

There is no good evidence that red wine improves cholesterol more than other drinks containing the same amount of alcohol. Red wine does contain polyphenols such as resveratrol, but the amounts are small. Its effects on blood fats come mainly from the alcohol, which raises triglycerides as well as HDL.

**Does beer raise cholesterol?**

Beer has no cholesterol itself, but it adds alcohol and carbohydrate calories. Regular or heavy beer drinking can raise triglycerides and contribute to weight gain, which can worsen the rest of your cholesterol profile. Moderate amounts have similar effects to other drinks with the same alcohol content.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking a statin?**

Light to moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable for most people on a statin, but ask your doctor about your situation. Statin labels caution against use in people who drink substantial amounts or have liver disease, and heavy drinking works against the drug by raising triglycerides and blood pressure.

**Will quitting alcohol lower my cholesterol?**

It usually lowers triglycerides, often within a few weeks, and helps with liver fat, blood pressure, and weight. HDL may drop slightly, which is expected. LDL often changes little unless quitting also leads to weight loss and better eating habits.

**Does DHM lower cholesterol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers cholesterol or triglycerides in people who drink. One small trial in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease reported improvements in some blood fat markers, but that hasn't been confirmed in larger studies. DHM does not replace drinking less or cholesterol medication.
